Values

Penn State Principles
The Pennsylvania State University is a community dedicated to personal and academic excellence. The Penn State Principles were developed to embody the values that we hope our students, faculty, staff, administration, and alumni possess. At the same time, the University is strongly committed to freedom of expression. Consequently, these Principles do not constitute University policy and are not intended to interfere in any way with an individual’s academic or personal freedoms. We hope, however, that individuals will voluntarily endorse these common principles, thereby contributing to the traditions and scholarly heritage left by those who preceded them, and will thus leave Penn State a better place for those who follow.
I will respect the dignity of all individuals within the Penn State community. The University is committed to creating and maintaining an educational environment that respects the right of all individuals to participate fully in the community. Actions motivated by hate, prejudice, or intolerance violate this principle. I will not engage in any behaviors that compromise or demean the dignity of individuals or groups, including intimidation, stalking, harassment, discrimination, taunting, ridiculing, insulting, or acts of violence. I will demonstrate respect for others by striving to learn from differences between people, ideas, and opinions and by avoiding behaviors that inhibit the ability of other community members to feel safe or welcome as they pursue their academic goals.
I will practice academic integrity. Academic integrity is a basic guiding principle for all academic activity at Penn State University, allowing the pursuit of scholarly activity in an open, honest, and responsible manner. In accordance with the University Code of Conduct, I will practice integrity in regard to all academic assignments. I will not engage in or tolerate acts of falsification, misrepresentation or deception because such acts of dishonesty violate the fundamental ethical principles of the University community and compromise the worth of work completed by others.
I will demonstrate social and personal responsibility. The University is a community that promotes learning; any behaviors that are inconsistent with that goal are unacceptable. Irresponsible behaviors, including alcohol or drug abuse and the use of violence against people or property, undermine the educational climate by threatening the physical and mental health of members of the community. I will exercise personal responsibility for my actions and I will make sure that my actions do not interfere with the academic and social environment of the University. I will maintain a high standard of behavior by adhering to the Code of Conduct and respecting the rights of others.
I will be responsible for my own academic progress and agree to comply with all University policies. The University allows students to identify and achieve their academic goals by providing the information needed to plan the chosen program of study and the necessary educational opportunities, but students assume final responsibility for course scheduling, program planning, and the successful completion of graduation requirements. I will be responsible for seeking the academic and career information needed to meet my educational goals by becoming knowledgeable about the relevant policies, procedures, and rules of the University and academic program, by consulting and meeting with my adviser, and by successfully completing all of the requirements for graduation.


Penn State Values
Integrity: We act with integrity and honesty in accordance with the highest academic, professional, and ethical standards.
Respect: We respect and honor the dignity of each person, embrace civil discourse, and foster a diverse and inclusive community.
Responsibility: We act responsibly, and we are accountable for our decisions, actions, and their consequences.
Discovery: We seek and create new knowledge and understanding, and foster creativity and innovation, for the benefit of our communities, society, and the environment.
Excellence: We strive for excellence in all our endeavors as individuals, an institution, and a leader in higher education.
Community: We work together for the betterment of our University, the communities we serve, and the world.

title: Tidying data
text: This tutorial shows how we can prepare a dataset generated using Google Forms into a format suitable for plotting. The format is a data frame in a “tidy” format, where each row is an observation and each column is a variable.

title: Tidying data
text: This tutorial shows how we can prepare a dataset generated using Google Forms into a format suitable for plotting. The format is a data frame in a “tidy” format, where each row is an observation and each column is a variable.

title: Tidying data
text:
Setup


Code
# Load required package dependencies "quietly"
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(readr))


If you are following this tutorial, you will want to do the following:

Create an RStudio project called tutorial-tidying-data or something similar.
Create a Quarto document inside the project.

Modify the title in the document header.
Add author, and date fields in the document header.
Optionally add parameters so that your HTML document is self-contained.
Add About and Setup sections to your main document and fill them with content, especially the R chunk you will use to load the required packages like ggplot2, readr, and dplyr using library(ggplot2) etc.

title: Tidying data
text:
Background
Even when a data analyst controls how some dataset is generated, it’s essential to transform it into a form that can be easily plotted using ggplot2.
The major steps involved are as follows:

Gathering

Importing the data from some canonical source.

Cleaning

(Optional, but highly recommended) Creating a data dictionary.
Transforming the data into a tidy format.
Renaming data variable (column) names.

Visualizing

We will do this with some survey data that Dr. Gilmore created. For Exercise 05, you’ll do the same process with the data you created in Exercise 03.
The response form for the survey is here: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/1-3A8QFqwNABsbOmCAgnrcdjxXULp-aKOW1HqQvPVd3k/edit. If you like the shortened form Google provides, it is here: https://forms.gle/add8aEUUjMowesaQ6.

title: Tidying data
text:
Gathering
There are two ways to gather these data. One involves downloading a *.csv file manually. If you visit the “Responses” tab for a survey you have permission to access, you’ll see a “View in Sheets” button as shown in Figure 1.






Figure 1: Screenshot of the Responses tab of the sample dataset.



Click it.
That will open a Google Sheet with the data as shown in Figure 2.






ImportantSample data file



You can download this datafile at the following link:
https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1ecLcV1IPGf2UyJKWHH6s81iG0vuiqJJaCELi9di_KHQ/edit?usp=sharing








Figure 2: Screen shot of the sample data file as of 2026-10-12.



On 2026-10-12 when I drafted this tutorial, there were 5 responses.
To download a CSV, select “File/Download/Comma Separated Values (.csv)” as shown in Figure 3.






Figure 3: Google Sheets menu command to generate and download a .csv file.



This will download the file to the default download location on your computer. The precise file name depends on how many times you’ve downloaded this file, but on my computer right now, the following code shows the long target file name.


Code
list.files(path = "~/Downloads",
           pattern = "PSYCH 490.007",
           full.names = TRUE)


[1] "/Users/rog1/Downloads/PSYCH 490.007 Ex-05 (Responses) - Form Responses 1.csv"








NoteWhat are those parameters?



For this exercise, you don’t need to automate determining the file name using the list.files() function. However, the path parameter tells R where to look for files. Here, it’s in the Downloads directory under my root user account which I appreviate using the ~ symbol. Note: This works on Mac OS and Linux systems, but I’m not sure it works like this in Windows.
The pattern parameter tells R to look for the text ‘PSYCH 490.007’. That’s how the file name starts.


Now that we’ve confirmed we have downloaded a .csv file, we can drag it to the folder where we’re doing our work. I suggest creating a data/csv folder for your data. Make a directory for the data and copy the file there now.
If you want to use R for this, the following code should work.


Code
dir.create(file.path("data"))
dir.create(file.path("data", "csv"))



Import into R
Now we can import the data into R. Create a chunk to do that. Call the data survey_df.


Code
survey_df <- read_csv("data/csv/PSYCH 490.007 Ex-05 (Responses) - Form Responses 1.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)








ImportantType-ahead is your friend



If you pause your typing after you type the first few characters of the path to your file, RStudio will fill in the rest.
In fact, type-ahead helps in all sorts of ways.
Slow down, let the computer do more work, and enjoy the good life!


To confirm that the dataset imported properly, we run summary(survey_df).


Code
summary(survey_df)


     Timestamp  What is your name?
 Length   : 5   Length   : 5      
 N.unique : 5   N.unique : 4      
 N.blank  : 0   N.blank  : 0      
 Min.nchar:17   Min.nchar: 7      
 Max.nchar:19   Max.nchar:10      
                                  
 What is the air speed of a fully laden swallow (in m/s)?
 Min.   : 1.0                                            
 1st Qu.: 5.5                                            
 Median :15.0                                            
 Mean   :18.1                                            
 3rd Qu.:25.0                                            
 Max.   :44.0                                            
 What is your favorite date (month, day, year)?
 Length   : 5                                  
 N.unique : 5                                  
 N.blank  : 0                                  
 Min.nchar: 9                                  
 Max.nchar:10                                  
                                               


An even more useful command to summarize the data is the str() for “structure” command.


Code
str(survey_df)


spc_tbl_ [5 × 4] (S3: spec_tbl_df/tbl_df/tbl/data.frame)
 $ Timestamp                                               : chr [1:5] "10/6/2026 7:47:36" "10/6/2026 7:47:44" "10/6/2026 7:47:53" "10/6/2026 7:48:08" ...
 $ What is your name?                                      : chr [1:5] "Puddintane" "Mayflower" "Janeway" "Aragorn" ...
 $ What is the air speed of a fully laden swallow (in m/s)?: num [1:5] 25 15 1 44 5.5
 $ What is your favorite date (month, day, year)?          : chr [1:5] "01/17/1993" "03/18/1965" "06/02/1981" "07/04/1776" ...
 - attr(*, "spec")=
  .. cols(
  ..   Timestamp = col_character(),
  ..   `What is your name?` = col_character(),
  ..   `What is the air speed of a fully laden swallow (in m/s)?` = col_double(),
  ..   `What is your favorite date (month, day, year)?` = col_character()
  .. )
 - attr(*, "problems")=<pointer: 0xb20cf0100> 


Notice that this command provides us even more information than we had before.
Okay, we’re ready to move on to cleaning.

title: Tidying data
text:
Cleaning

Make data dictionary
Until very recently, I never made a data dictionary. I didn’t know what one was or why someone should care. Fortunately, you can teach (some) old dogs new tricks.
It’s optional for Exercise 05, but worth extra points, so why not?
First, we extract the full questions using the names() command. This command extracts the column names from a data frame. We assign it to a variable because we’ll want to use it in our data dictionary.


Code
questions <- names(survey_df)
questions


[1] "Timestamp"                                               
[2] "What is your name?"                                      
[3] "What is the air speed of a fully laden swallow (in m/s)?"
[4] "What is your favorite date (month, day, year)?"          


Next, we create a new variable with a shortened name. The question itself is too long. We want a name that will be informative, but look good in our initial plots.
Here are the choices I made:


Code
short_names <- c("timestamp",
                "name",
                "swallow_speed",
                "favorite_date")


Now, I can make a new data frame with the questions and short_names variables.


Code
survey_dd <- data.frame(questions, short_names)

survey_dd


                                                 questions   short_names
1                                                Timestamp     timestamp
2                                       What is your name?          name
3 What is the air speed of a fully laden swallow (in m/s)? swallow_speed
4           What is your favorite date (month, day, year)? favorite_date


That’s not especially interesting, but so far so good. You could add other columns if you like. A comments column isn’t a bad idea.


Code
comments <- c("Provided by Google Forms in MM/DD/YYYY HH:MM:SS format",
              "Fixed responses",
              "A bad reference to 'Monty Python and the Holy Grail'.",
              "Some random dates in MM/DD/YY format.")


And you could add a column about the data type.


Code
data_type <- c("Date/time stamp", 
               "Discrete/Nominal",
               "Continuous",
               "Date")


Then add these to the data dictionary data frame.


Code
survey_dd$data_type <- data_type
survey_dd$comments <- comments
survey_dd


                                                 questions   short_names
1                                                Timestamp     timestamp
2                                       What is your name?          name
3 What is the air speed of a fully laden swallow (in m/s)? swallow_speed
4           What is your favorite date (month, day, year)? favorite_date
         data_type                                               comments
1  Date/time stamp Provided by Google Forms in MM/DD/YYYY HH:MM:SS format
2 Discrete/Nominal                                        Fixed responses
3       Continuous  A bad reference to 'Monty Python and the Holy Grail'.
4             Date                  Some random dates in MM/DD/YY format.


Let’s quit while we’re ahead and export this as a .csv in the same directory where our raw data came from, but with a shorter and human-readable name.


Code
write_csv(survey_dd, file = "data/csv/survey_data_dictionary.csv")


Okay, back to data cleaning the main dataset.


Rename columns
As part of generating the data dictionary, we made choices about some better, shorter names for the columns in our dataset. We can use those names in the raw dataset, as follows.
First, we make a copy of survey_df, but with a new name to indicate it’s our cleaned version. This isn’t strictly necessary, but it’s good practice while you’re learning.


Code
survey_cleaned_df <- survey_df


Then, we give the new dataset, survey_cleaned_df the short names from our data dictionary.


Code
names(survey_cleaned_df) <- short_names

survey_cleaned_df


# A tibble: 5 × 4
  timestamp           name       swallow_speed favorite_date
  <chr>               <chr>              <dbl> <chr>        
1 10/6/2026 7:47:36   Puddintane          25   01/17/1993   
2 10/6/2026 7:47:44   Mayflower           15   03/18/1965   
3 10/6/2026 7:47:53   Janeway              1   06/02/1981   
4 10/6/2026 7:48:08   Aragorn             44   07/04/1776   
5 10/12/2026 11:45:34 Janeway              5.5 7/13/1997    








ImportantStudy this and understand



Make sure you understand what we just did. It’s incredibly useful and powerful.
If you’re not sure what’s going on, try printing the original and the cleaned data frames, like this:


Code
survey_cleaned_df

survey_df


Compare the two outputs. Isn’t the one with shorter names easier to handle?




Further cleaning
We have two variables we could plot right now, name, and swallow_speed. In the section below we create simple visualizations of these variables.


Alternative method
If you don’t want to make a data dictionary, there is another way to rename variables in a data frame. We use a function from the dplyr package called rename().
First, make sure that you have installed dplyr. In your R console, run install.packages("dplyr"). Then, load the package by adding library(dplyr) to your setup section R chunk.
Now, we’re ready to use rename().
In the code below, we “pipe” (|>) the original survey data (survey_df) to the rename() function, then assign (<-) the output to a new data frame called survey_df_renamed. Notice that the rename() function takes a data frame and returns a new data frame with renamed columns. The rename() function also allows you to specify new column names using a formula-like syntax, such as new_name = old_name. Here, because our old names contain spaces, we surround them with back ticks so that dplyr will understand. We can rename multiple variables using the same command if we separate each new_name = \old name`` by a comma.






ImportantExpert tip: Use code formatting



RStudio will reformat your code for you to make it more human readable.
Select the section of code you want to reformat, then select the “Reformat section” command from the RStudio “Code” menu.



survey_df_renamed <- survey_df |>
  rename(
    timestamp = `Timestamp`,
    name = `What is your name?`,
    swallow_speed = `What is the air speed of a fully laden swallow (in m/s)?`,
    favorite_date = `What is your favorite date (month, day, year)?`
  )

survey_df_renamed

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  timestamp           name       swallow_speed favorite_date
  <chr>               <chr>              <dbl> <chr>        
1 10/6/2026 7:47:36   Puddintane          25   01/17/1993   
2 10/6/2026 7:47:44   Mayflower           15   03/18/1965   
3 10/6/2026 7:47:53   Janeway              1   06/02/1981   
4 10/6/2026 7:48:08   Aragorn             44   07/04/1776   
5 10/12/2026 11:45:34 Janeway              5.5 7/13/1997    


Notice that this gives us the same result as before.






NoteWhat technique to use when?



Should you create a data dictionary and use the short_name field to reassign new names to your original data frame, or should you use the dplyr::rename() function we just demonstrated? As with many (most?) things in life, the answer is: It depends. I use both.
Creating a data dictionary is a best practice for organizing and documenting your data, especially when working with complex datasets or collaborating with others. However, you may just want to rename variables and get on with your work.
For work in this class, especially on Exercise 05, you decide. Maybe try the rename() function for this tutorial but snag the extra credit points for Exercise 05 by making a data dictionary.

title: Tidying data
text:
Visualizing
We’ve already used summary() and str() above, so we won’t repeat that here. Notice that in Figure 4 we use the cleaned dataset. Also note that we can use geom_histogram with discrete, nominal data as long as we use stat="count" as a parameter.


Code
survey_cleaned_df |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = name) +
  geom_histogram(stat = "count") +
  theme_classic()


Warning in geom_histogram(stat = "count"): Ignoring unknown parameters:
`binwidth` and `bins`








Figure 4: A simple barplot of the frequency of responses to the question: ‘What is your name?’











ImportantMake this better



What would make this figure more informative and compelling?
How about sorting the bars, adding some color, adding a better title?


In Figure 5, we plot the swallow_speed variable.


Code
survey_cleaned_df |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = swallow_speed) +
  geom_histogram() +
  theme_classic()


`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.








Figure 5: A histogram of responses to the question: ‘What is the air speed of a fully laden swallow (in m/s)?’





This specific figure is not very appealing or informative because we have too few data points for a histogram. But it shows how we can go from raw data to some visualizations in just a few steps. When you make figures from your own data in Exercise 05, you may discover that some datasets don’t work especially well with certain figure types. This is why I recommend using Quarto and code chunks to make different versions of your figures. It’s a way to build upon previous work AND keep track of the history of your exploration.

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
This tutorial shows how to use additional commands in ggplot2 to customize figures.
I recommend that you create your own RStudio project with a new Quarto document to work through this tutorial.

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
2 Setup


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)



Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
3 Acquire data
Let’s make some continuous data that have different degrees of relatedness.

n_pts = 600
x <- rnorm(n = n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 1)
y_25 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 0.25)
y_50 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 0.50)
y_75 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 0.75)
y_100 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 1)
y_125 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 1.25)
y_150 <- x + rnorm(n_pts, mean = 0, sd = 1.50)

df <- data.frame(x = rep(x, 6), 
                 y = c(y_25, y_50, y_75, y_100, y_125, y_150), 
                 noise = c(.25, .50, .75, 1.00, 1.25, 1.50), 
                 each = n_pts)







ImportantChange any variable you like



One powerful way to learn a new skill is to take sample code, alter it, and see what happens. Here, you could change the n_pts variable to see how the figures look with different number of points.

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
4 Visualize

4.1 Basic scatterplot
In Figure 1, I filter the bigger dataset using the filter(noise == 0.25) command. This selects the subset where the noise is 0.25.






NoteTroubleshooting



Make sure that your Quarto document’s Setup chunk has library(dplyr) in it. Alternatively, you could change the filter(noise == 0.25) line to dplyr::filter(noise == 0.25). This tells R to find and use dplyr even if you haven’t run library(dplyr) in your Quarto document.
If this fails, then you may need to install dplyr. In your R console, outside of your Quarto document, run install.packages("dplyr"). Then go back and render your Quarto document.
Think of the problem this way. Let’s say that your friend says “I have to call Mike.” But you know lots of Mike’s, so unless it’s obvious from context which Mike you’re talking about, things could go sideways. By telling R library(dplyr), we’re saying that we’re talking about filter() from the dplyr package, not some other filter() command.



df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point()







Figure 1







4.2 Adjust alpha
In Figure 2 I try reducing clutter by adjusting alpha. The alpha parameter controls the saturation (intensity) of the dots based on how many points overlap. Lower values of alpha mean that more points have to overlap for that point to appear darker or more saturated. Notice that the alpha parameter belongs with geom_point(). If we had other layers, say lines or annotations, these could have their own alpha levels.
Here I tried alpha = 0.3.

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3)







Figure 2

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
5 Change theme
In Figure 3 I eliminate the gray background, by adding a theme. There are many ggplot2 themes, but theme_classic() is a decent place to start.

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  theme_classic()







Figure 3

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
6 Add labels
In Figure 4, I keep the previous changes and add some labels using labs(), short for labels. Notice that the labs() function has a parameter for title, subtitle, and caption.

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, .25).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.")







Figure 4






6.1 Change text size
The text is small. In Figure 5, I adjust it with another theme() command.

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, .25).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))







Figure 5





Read the help document about the labs() command to learn more. Enter help("labs") into your R console.

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
7 Add best-fitting line
In Figure 6 we add a best-fitting line using geom_smooth(method = "lm").

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.",
       subtitle = "y = x + N(0, .25).",
       caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 6

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
8 Add annotation
In Figure 7 we add an annotations featuring the the correlation (r value) using annotate().

xy_corr <- with(df, cor.test(x, y))

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.",
       subtitle = "y = x + N(0, .25).",
       caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate("text",
           x = -2,
           y = 3,
           label = "r = .89") +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 7






8.1 Grab correlation
Add an annotation with the correlation using annotate(), but grab the correlation from a variable.

xy_corr <- with(df, cor.test(x, y))

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.",
       subtitle = "y = x + N(0, .25).",
       caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = -1,
    y = 3,
    label = paste0("r = ", xy_corr$estimate)
  ) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 8











ImportantWhat the coordinates mean in annotate()



You might notice that the x and y coordinates we give to the annotate() layer specify the middle point of the text for our annotation.




8.2 Format annotation
The correlation value has too many digits, so let’s fix that.

xy_corr <- with(df, cor.test(x,y))
corr_r <- xy_corr$estimate |>
  format(digits = 3)

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, .25).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate("text", x = -2, y = 3, label = paste0("r = ", corr_r)) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 9







8.3 Extend annotation
Add a p value and degrees of freedom to the annotation.

df_25 <- filter(df, noise == .25)

xy_corr <- with(df_25, cor.test(x,y))
corr_r <- xy_corr$estimate |>
  format(digits = 3)
sample_n <- xy_corr$parameter
p_value <- format(xy_corr$p.value, digits = 3)
est_lo <- format(xy_corr$conf.int[1], digits = 2)
est_hi <- format(xy_corr$conf.int[2], digits = 2)

corr_text <- paste0("r(", sample_n, ")=", corr_r, ", p=", p_value)

df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, .25).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate("text", x = -2, y = 3.75, label = corr_text) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 10







8.4 Different noise level
Let’s try one with a different noise level.

df_150 <- filter(df, noise == 1.50)

xy_corr <- with(df_150, cor.test(x,y))
corr_r <- xy_corr$estimate |>
  format(digits = 3)
sample_n <- xy_corr$parameter
p_value <- format(xy_corr$p.value, digits = 3)
est_lo <- format(xy_corr$conf.int[1], digits = 2)
est_hi <- format(xy_corr$conf.int[2], digits = 2)

corr_text <- paste0("r(", sample_n, ")=", corr_r, ", p=", p_value)

df_150 |>
  # filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line.", subtitle= "y = x + N(0, 1.50).", caption = "The data show an expected strong linear relationship.") +
  annotate("text", x = -2, y = 3.75, label = corr_text) +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 11

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
9 Facets
Let’s take the gist of Figure 9 and make a plot with multiple facets based on the amount of random noise added to y.

df_categorical_noise <- df |>
  mutate(noise_cat = ordered(noise))

df_categorical_noise |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point(alpha = .1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  facet_wrap(facets = ~ noise_cat, ncol = 3) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(title = "A scatter plot with random data and a best-fitting line at various levels of random noise.") +
  theme(title = element_text(size = 14))

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 12

title: Tutorial: Customizing ggplot figures
text:
10 Assigning names
In the next series of figures, we’ll take advantage of a cool feature of the ggplot2 syntax: Assigning figures to a variable. This can make the process of exploring different figure options much easier.
So, in Figure 13 below we give a very basic plot a name: p.

p <- df |>
  filter(noise == .25) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x, y) +
  geom_point()

p







Figure 13





Now, we can “add” new layers or themese to the base figure using the syntax indicated below.

10.1 Add a layer

p + theme_classic()

p_classic <- p + theme_classic()







Figure 14







10.2 Add a line
Figure 15 adds a smooth, best-fitting line to Figure 14. Note that in the previous code gave Figure 14 the name p_classic. This let’s us “add” the geom_smooth() to p_classic as indicated below.

p_classic + geom_smooth(method = "lm")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 15







10.3 Dark theme
We can use this syntax to explore the space of features we want for our plot. Figure 16 tries theme_dark().

p + theme_dark() + geom_smooth(method = "lm")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 16







10.4 Light theme
Figure 17 tries theme_light().

p + theme_light() + geom_smooth(method = "lm")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'








Figure 17

title: ggplot2 tutorial I
text:
Install ggplot2
Base R has many useful functions, but ggplot2 is not one of them. So, you will need to install it using the install.packages() function.
Switch to the R console, and install the package as follows:
install.packages("ggplot2")
You’ll only need to do this once.

title: ggplot2 tutorial I
text:
Quarto as a lab notebook
We’re going to use Quarto as a lab notebook.
Each time we start a new thing, we’re going to start a new section in our document.

Add a Setup section
This is a good time to add a setup section to your document. This section is where get ready to do real work.
So, add a chunk like this after your About section:
## Setup
Below the setup header, we’re going to add an R code chunk like this:
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
```
The library() command brings the package into the computational environment1 and lets us call the other functions and commands in ggplot2 by their “first” names.

title: ggplot2 tutorial I
text:
Our first plot
Add a new section called My First Plot or Figure 01 or something like that.
## Figure 01
Then you might add some text explaining what the first plot is about. For example, you could describe the data being visualized and the purpose of the plot.
Here, we’re going to use the diamonds dataset the is built in to ggplot2.
Create an R chunk as follows:



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = price) +
  geom_histogram()
```


Figure 6: Simple ggplot2 syntax to plot a histogram of the price variable in the diamonds dataset.









WarningSyntax slip-ups



90+% of frustrations with computers are because we don’t tell them exactly what they need to know.
A code chunk in Quarto starts with triple backticks and ends with triple backticks.
The {r} tells Quarto that the code chunk is written in R.
Quarto understands other programming languages, so this is important.


Save and render your Quarto document.


`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.








Figure 7: Output of code in Figure 6.





The resulting web page should look something like this:






Figure 8: Quarto document rendered after Figure 01 code is executed.




Unpacking ggplot syntax
To make a figure, we need a dataset formatted as a data frame. The diamonds dataset is already in the right format.
In our plotting code illustrated in Figure 6, we call the ggplot() function and specify the dataset to plot using the data=diamonds parameter2.
Next, we ‘add’ a layer to our figure using the + command. That layer contains the ‘aesthetics’ or mapping between our dataset and some feature of the figure (e.g., x position, y position, fill color, etc.) We specify these mappings using the aes() command. For this specific figure, we’re mapping x position on the figure to the price variable in the dataset.
Finally, our figure needs a ‘geom’, a geometric object or format for the figure. We have a single variable (price), and we want to plot a histogram of it, so we add (+) use the geom_histogram().

title: ggplot2 tutorial I
text:
Another variable
Let’s plot another variable from the diamonds datasets.
Create a new subsection called Figure 02 in your Quarto document, then create a new code chunk in your Quarto document with the following code:



```{r}
head(diamonds)
```


Figure 9: Code to show the ‘head’ of the diamonds dataset.

The head() command outputs the first few rows of a data frame. This is useful for quickly inspecting the structure and contents of the data.
Let’s make a histogram of the carat variable. Make a new R chunk in your Quarto file; copy the Figure 1 code to the chunk; change the x value in the aes() function to read aes(x = carat ).



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = carat) +
  geom_histogram()
```


Figure 10: Code to generate a histogram of the carat variable from the diamonds dataset.



Save and render the Quarto document.


`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.








Figure 11: Output of the code in Figure 10

title: ggplot2 tutorial I
text:
Violin plots
There are other ‘geoms’ we can use with continuous data like price and carat. A violin plot is one of them.
Again, make a new Figure 03 section in your Quarto document. Then, make a new code chunk with the following:



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = price, y = "") +
  geom_violin()
  
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = carat, y = "") +
  geom_violin()
```


Figure 12: Code to create violin plots of both the price and carat variables.



Yes, this should make two different violin plots.
Save and render the Quarto document








Figure 13: Output from the code chunk in Figure 12.











Figure 14: Output from the code chunk in Figure 12.





Notice that geom_violin() requires us to specify both x and y aesthetics even if we only want to plot one variable. We tell ggplot to ignore the other mapping by setting y="".

title: ggplot2 tutorial I
text:
Scatterplots
Let’s make a scatterplot of price and carat using geom_point and set the x and y aesthetics. That will put price on the x or horizontal axis and carat on the y or vertical axis. You could switch them; it doesn’t really matter.
Make a Figure 04 section in your Quarto document, then add a code chunk with the following:



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = price, y = carat) +
  geom_point()
```


Figure 15: Code to create a scatterplot of the price and carat variables from the diamonds dataset.











Figure 16: Output from the prior code chunk.

title: ggplot2 tutorial I
text:
Multiple violin plots
If you want to push yourself, add a Figure 05 section with the following code chunk. Save and render the document, then explain what’s going on with the figure.



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = price, y = cut, color = cut, fill = cut) +
  geom_violin() +
  xlab("Price in $") +
  ylab("Cut of diamond") +
  ggtitle("Price vs. Cut")
```


Figure 17: Code to generate multiple violin plots, one for each value of the discrete (ordinal) variable cut. Note the use of new aesthetics fill and color, customized axis labels using xlab() and ylab() and a title using ggtitle().











Figure 18: Output from the prior code chunk.

title: ggplot2 tutorial I
text:
Combination plot
Let’s implement a version of the combination plot from the Making and visualizing data tutorial.
Create a Figure 06 section in your Quarto document, add this chunk of code, save, and render.



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = price, y = "") +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .4) +
  ylab("")
```


Figure 19: Code to generate combination plot of diamonds price data.











Figure 20: Output from the code in Figure 19.











ImportantWhat are those new parameters?



Note that there is an alpha parameter in the geom_boxplot() function in Figure 19. What does it do?
One way to answer this is to create new versions of the figures with different values of alpha. You could do this by creating new subsections in your Quarto document, say one like this:
### `alpha = 1`

The following figure shows what happens to Figure 06 when we set `alpha` in `geom_boxplot` to 1.
Then, copy the Figure 06 code to a new code chunk but change the alpha value.
So, what does alpha do?

text:
Gathering
Next, we download the data from the Google Sheet where it is collected. Dr. Gilmore has stored his Google account credentials in a special environment file that can be accessed by the R command Sys.getenv("GMAIL_SURVEY").






Tip



It’s vital to be very careful when creating and sharing code like this that involves sensitive information like login credentials.
Gilmore likes to put credentials in an .Renviron file that lives in his home directory. This is a recommended practice. On Mac OS and Linux, that’s ~/.Renviron. You can use the usethis::edit_r_profile() command at the R console (not the Terminal) to open your own .Renviron file. In Gilmore’s case, he has added the following line to that file:
GMAIL_SURVEY="<my-google-account>"
Here, he has substituted his Google account with credentials/access to the required files for <my-google-account>. Then, when the R code below calls Sys.getenv("GMAIL_SURVEY"), the value of those credentials is returned as a text string.
Make sure to close and save the .Renviron file and restart your R session before testing this yourself.




Code
if (!dir.exists('csv')) {
  message("Creating missing `csv/`.")
  dir.create("csv")
}

if (params$update_data) {
  options(gargle_oauth_email = Sys.getenv("GMAIL_SURVEY"))
  googledrive::drive_auth()

  googledrive::drive_download(
    "PSYCH-490.007-2026-Fall-Psych-Viz",
    path = file.path("csv", params$fn),
    type = "csv",
    overwrite = TRUE
  )
  message("Data updated.")
} else {
  message("Using stored data.")
}


The data file has been saved as a comma-separated value (CSV) format data file in a special directory called csv/.






Note



Because these data might contain sensitive or identifiable information, we only keep a local copy and do not share it publicly via GitHub. This is achieved by adding the name of the data directory to a special .gitignore file.

title: PSYCH 490.007: Exercise 04
text:
This page documents Rick Gilmore’s work related to completing Exercise 04 for PSYCH 490.007 in Fall 2026.
The assignment involves choosing an existing dataset and making at least three (3) visualizations using the ggplot2 package. For each figure, I am to write a short summary of the question I intend to ask with the figure, and how the visualization I generate answers or doesn’t answer the question. If my figure doesn’t clearly answer the question, then I should explain how the figure might be improved or clarified to do so. This critique could include a suggestion to use a different type of figure.

title: PSYCH 490.007: Exercise 04
text:
Make figures

Figure 1
This figure shows a violin plot of home team scores. It should show whether there is a modal (most common) value.


Code
nfl_scheds |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = home_score) +
  geom_violin()


Warning: Removed 178 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range
(`stat_ydensity()`).








Figure 1





The violin shape is widest between 20 and about 25, indicating that scores in this range are the most common.
I could confirm this with the following R code:


Code
with(nfl_scheds, summary(home_score))


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.     NAs 
    0.0    16.0    23.0    23.3    30.0    70.0     178 


Sure enough, the mean is 23.3 and the median 23.


Figure 2
For Figure 2, I decided to try to plot my own version of a figure I linked to in Exercise 02.
Here is the figure from Exercise 02:






Figure 2: Figure 1 from https://www.psychologicalscience.org/redesign/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/TCD_fig_1.jpg



Here is the figure I made:


Code
age <- seq(from=3, to = 18)
mean_t <- c(54, 54, 54, 52, 51, 50.5, 49.5, 49, 48, 47.5, 47.25, 46, 45, 44.5, 44, 45)
sex = rep("male", length(age))

activity <- data.frame(age, mean_t)

activity |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = age, y = mean_t, color = sex) +
  geom_line()








Figure 3: Regenerating Figure 1 from https://www.psychologicalscience.org/redesign/wp-content/uploads/2015/12/TCD_fig_1.jpg





Note that I only show the male data. I had to enter the data by hand, and I got tired of that. You get the general idea.

title: Making tables

Wait! You said Base R

I did, but I wanted to select two variables from mtcars.
The select function from dplyr does that easily.
Note: These slides did not start with a setup chunk

So, no library(dplyr) statement
But I can access the dplyr commands with dplyr::<command>.

title: Making tables
text:
Under the hood

To make tables with titles and sequential numbers using Quarto…

```{r}
#| label: tbl-cyl-gear
#| tbl-cap: "Number of cars in the *mtcars* dataset by the number of cylinders in the engine and the number of gears in the transmission."
mtcars |>
  dplyr::select(cyl, gear) |>
  table()
```

Give your R chunk a label starting with tbl-
Add a tbl-cap for the caption
Then you can link to the table, for example Table 3

title: Making tables
text:
Making a summary table

variables <- c("mpg", "disp")
mins <- c(min(mtcars$mpg), 
          min(mtcars$disp))
meds <- c(median(mtcars$mpg), 
          median(mtcars$disp))
means <- c(mean(mtcars$mpg), 
           mean(mtcars$disp))
maxs <- c(max(mtcars$mpg), 
          max(mtcars$disp))

my_stats_df <- data.frame(variable = variables,
                       min = mins,
                       median = meds,
                       mean = means,
                       max = maxs)

Some take-homes

Data frames are useful and flexible structures
The custom summary table is similar to the data dictionary we made in the Tidying Data tutorial.

title: Making tables
text:
Main points

Tables can be informative accompaniments to figures
Data frames are useful and flexible structures for making both
Think about the kind of table you want to produce
Making pretty tables in R can be done; we’re getting there
Scripting the generation of tables makes them less error-prone

title: Making maps with data: Part II
text:
Higher ed data

Create a nominal (ordinal) variable called tier based on the number of institutions


pa_map_sf_tiers <- pa_map_sf |>
  mutate(
    tier = case_when(
      is.na(n_institutions) ~ "none",
      n_institutions <= 5 ~ "<=5",
      n_institutions <= 10 ~ "6-10",
      n_institutions <= 15 ~ "11-15",
      n_institutions < 21 ~ "16-20"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(tier = ordered(tier, 
                        levels = c("none", "<=5", "6-10", 
                                   "11-15", "16-20")))

title: Making maps with data: Part II
text:
Higher ed data

Plot the data by tier


pa_map_sf_tiers |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = tier), color = "white", size = 0.1) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "County-Level Choropleth Map",
       subtitle = "PA Counties Colored by number of higher ed institutions",
       caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau / tigris")

Some datasets are available to you without doing anything special, e.g., mtcars.

title: Work session: Making figures on your own

A best practice to adopt is to explain your choices. So, if you use a dataset built in to R, say that’s what you did. If you choose a package that must be loaded from another source, explain that.

title: Work session: Making figures on your own
text:
## Figure 1

In this figure, I will plot the <variable> from the <dataset> dataset.
The variable is continuous, so I will use a <plot_type> that should show me...

```{r}
#| label: fig-01
dataset |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = variable) +
  
```

title: Work session: Making figures on your own
text:
Figure numbering is optional


Note that the code chunk on the previous page added #| label: fig-01 before the actual code.
This tells Quarto to add a figure number automatically.
If you get this to work, bravo!
The main benefit is that you can now write @fig-01 in your text, and Quarto will create a link to the figure.
So, your Figure 1 section could look like the following.

title: Figure components
text:
Meals eaten vs. not-eaten

See slides from 2026-09-11, 2026-09-14.



Code
days <- factor(
  c("sun", "mon", "tue", "wed", "thu", "fri", "sat"),
  levels = c("sun", "mon", "tue", "wed", "thu", "fri", "sat"),
  ordered = TRUE
)
meals <- factor(
  c("breakfast", "lunch", "dinner", "snack", "dessert"),
  levels = c("breakfast", "lunch", "snack", "dinner", "dessert"),
  ordered = TRUE
)
meal_days <- rep(days, each = length(meals))
weekly_meals <- rep(meals, 7)

my_meals <- data.frame(day_of_wk = meal_days, 
                       meal = weekly_meals)
ate_it <- sample(c(TRUE, FALSE), size = 35, 
                 replace = TRUE, prob = c(.6, .4))
my_meals$ate_it <- ate_it

meals_eaten <- my_meals$meal[my_meals$ate_it == TRUE]
meals_eaten_df <- data.frame(meal = meals_eaten)

title: Under the hood
text:
Workflow
The site is written in Quarto.
A site-wide YAML file (_quarto.yml) controls the rendering process.
Separate directories contain lecture slides (slides/), exercises (exercises/), class-specific R functions (R/), surveys (surveys/), and tutorials (tutorials/). Quarto files with underscores (e.g., _index.qmd, _about.qmd, _evaluation.qmd, _schedule.qmd, and values.qmd) are the main targets for editing and updating. Parent files (e.g., index.qmd, evaluation.qmd, policies.qmd, and schedule.qmd) call upon these child files in the rendering process.
A separate Quarto file (psych-490.007-2026-fall-syllabus.qmd) generates a PDF version of a syllabus.

title: Under the hood
text:
Rendering
To render the full site, quarto render src is executed from the command line. The fully rendered website is written to docs/.

title: Under the hood
text:
Software
The site uses the renv package to try to make all computation reproducible.
In addition, the site uses softbib to generate a full reference list of the package dependencies. This is saved in src/include/bib.

title: Final Project
text:
Components

Project proposal

Every student or team must submit a one-page single-spaced project proposal. Your proposal should state the aim or objective of your project, the format, and a include a brief description of how you intend to go about achieving your objectives.

The proposal is due on Thursday, March 6.


Project presentation

Every student or team may make an optional presentation to the class about their project. Please indicate whether you are willing to make a presentation when you complete the survey.
Note: Giving a presentation is worth 5 extra credit points.
The presentations will occur during class on December 7, 9, and 11.
If you wish to have your presentation made available publicly on the course website, please let me know. This is also completely optional.



Project write-up

Every student or team must submit a write-up, due during finals week on Wednesday, December 16.
Depending on the format of the project (talk, poster, paper), different written materials may be submitted (slides, poster, etc.).
For an in-class talk, submit a separate document with your talk text or notes and your slides. You may also submit slides that include presenter notes embedded within them.
For a poster, submit a PowerPoint or PDF of your poster along with any talking points.

Rubic: An example of potential grading template we may use: https://commons.erau.edu/db-srs/poster-scoring-rubric.pdf
Article: How to make a good scientific poster https://www.nature.com/articles/nj7614-115a
Tutorial video: how to make a poster https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EL5YwkiqBho&ab_channel=SamHertig
Other basics: https://guides.libraries.psu.edu/posters

For a research paper, please submit an APA-formatted manuscript 1,500-2,000 words in length (~ 7-10 double-spaced pages).
For an opinion piece, please submit a document up to 1,500 words in length.
For an interactive website or presentation, please submit a complete set of files needed to evaluate your website or presentation.
For a lesson plan, please submit a document up up to 1,500 words in length.

For 3 extra credit points, create a data dictionary file (as a .csv).

At a minimum, the data dictionary should include the “raw” questions, and the “short_name” you assigned to the variable.

Submit the .html file.

title: Exercise 03
text:
Assignment

Sign-in to the Google drive account associated with your Penn State Access ID. This will make it somewhat easier for us to share forms.
Open Google Forms by visiting https://forms.google.com.
Create a new form by clicking on the ‘Blank Form’ button.

 3. Give your form a useful title, for example, ‘PSYCH-490.007-2026-spring-team-A’ or ‘PSYCH-490.007-2026-spring-rog1’.






Important



You can be assigned a team name/letter if you choose.



Customize the theme if you wish by clicking on the palette icon.
Create a survey with 8 questions. Your questions should be ones that your classmates can answer without embarrassment or loss of privacy and which meet the following criteria:


Generate two questions with nominal (un-ordered) answers (e.g., favorite color).
Generate two questions with ordinal (e.g., 1-5) answers analogous to a Likert scale.
Generate two questions with continuous answers (e.g., age and shoe size). It doesn’t matter if these are interval or ratio scaled.
Generate one question with a date or time as an answer (e.g., a favorite relative’s birthday).

The city variable should contain the names of the cities; e.g., city = c("Pittsburgh", "State College") would be the start of my own list.
The lat and lon variables are the decimal latitude and longitude values for these locations. There are many ways to find these, including Google maps1. The status variable should contain a value for each city such as “lived_in”, “hope_to_visit”. I would start this for my own cities as follows: `status <- c(“lived_in”, “lived_in”).
If you follow the pattern above, then your data frame could be created as follows: my_travels <- data.frame(city, lat, lon, status).


Make a map of these locations using the sf, rnaturalearth, rnaturalearthdata, ggplot2, and dplyr packages.


Map the color or shape of the points on your plot to the status variable.

title: The Psychology of Data Visualization
text:
Themes
If a picture’s worth a thousand words (Wikipedia contributors, 2024), what exactly does it say? This course will focus on the psychology of data visualization—how to read, critique, and generate meaningful figures that inform but don’t mislead. We’ll take inspiration from recognized classic figures and unpack what makes them exemplary. We’ll critique figures that deliberately or inadvertently mislead or confuse. We’ll learn what 150 years of vision science, the foundation of experimental psychology, has to say about data visualization. And we’ll learn how to build our own reproducible figures using Python, R, and JavaScript. No prior programming experience is required.

Figure 2: A histogram of a random, normally distributed distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation of 1.

title: Work session: Introducing R & RStudio
text:
Code to generate this figure
# Generate a random normal distribution using the `rnorm()` function.
# Assign the distribution a name: `x_norm` so I can use it later.

x_norm <- rnorm(n = 100, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# "Pipe" `x_norm` to `ggplot2()` to make a histogram.

x_norm |>
  as.data.frame() |>          # ggplot requires a tabular data frame
  ggplot() +                  #  as input
  aes(x = x_norm) +
  geom_histogram()

title: Work session: Introducing R & RStudio
text:
Extra fun
install.packages("ggplot2")
library(ggplot2)

scatter_data <- data.frame(x_norm = rnorm(100, 0, 1),
                           y_norm = rnorm(100, 0, 1))

scatter_data |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = x_norm, y = y_norm) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth() +
  ggtitle("My first scatterplot!")

title: Intro to ggplot
text:
What is it?

R package that implements Wilkinson et al’s “grammar of graphics” (Wilkinson et al. 2005)

Written by Hadley Wickham, CTO of Posit.co

Maps data to figure components

Position (on axis)
Color (lines and fills), shape, size, texture

Add layers to figures, e.g., annotations

title: Intro to ggplot
text:
Why ‘code’ your figures?

Easier to reproduce
Easier to edit
Try out different styles, pick the best
Be kind to your future (forgetful) self
Makes programming more fun

title: Intro to ggplot
text:
Basic ggplot components

A data frame (rectangular dataset: rows are observations, named columns are variables)
Function call to ggplot()
Add layers to plot with + operator
Add aesthetics (mappings between data and graphic elements) using aes() with x (and often y) mappings
A geom_ layer

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Best practices



Each ggplot figure requires the following components at minimum:

Dataset, e.g. ggplot(data = ...) +
Aesthetic mapping(s): aes(x = ...) +



```{r}
#| label: fig-mtcars-wt-violin
ggplot(data = mtcars) +
  aes(x = wt) +
  geom_violin()
```

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Best practices



Each ggplot figure requires the following components at minimum:

A geom_, e.g., geom_histogram() or geom_violin()



```{r}
#| label: fig-mtcars-wt-violin
ggplot(data = mtcars) +
  aes(x = wt) +
  geom_violin()
```

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Best practices



The aesthetic(s) get “added” to the plot with the plus (+) character
So does the geom_


```{r}
#| label: fig-mtcars-wt-violin
ggplot(data = mtcars) +
  aes(x = wt) +
  geom_violin()
```









Figure 6

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Some bells & whistles



giphy.com

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Figure numbering is optional, but easy and useful


Note that the code chunk on the previous page added #| label: fig-mtcars-wt-violin before the actual code. The #| tells Quarto that these are parameters for this particular R code chunk. So, by saying #| label: we give the output figure from this chunk a unique name. Doing so tells Quarto to add a figure number automatically.
The main benefit is that you can now write @fig-mtcars-wt-violin in your text, and Quarto will create a link to the figure.
Here’s what I mean:
In the previous slide, we made a violin plot of the mtcars wt variable (Figure 6).
Slick, eh?

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Figure captions



Like figure numbering, figure captions are easy & extremely useful
Add #| fig-cap: "My figure caption" with your caption text below
Put it below the figure label and name, but above your actual code


```{r}
#| label: fig-mtcars-wt-boxplot
#| fig-cap: "A boxplot of the wt variable from the mtcars dataset."
ggplot(data = mtcars) +
  aes(x = wt) +
  geom_boxplot()
```









Figure 7: A boxplot of the wt variable from the mtcars dataset. Click to see larger image.

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Combining figure numbers & captions

Figure 6 shows a violin plot of the wt variable.
Figure 7 shows a boxplot of this variable.







Hover-able & clickable figure links


You may hover2 over any of the named figure links above to see a preview. Clicking takes you to the original page.

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Add color

If you’re tired of gray bars and black points, try the fill or color aesthetics.
geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "red") makes all bar outlines red.



Code
rx <- rnorm(100)
df <- data.frame(rx)
ggplot(df) +
  aes(x = rx) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, color = "red")

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Add color 3

You can map a discrete (nominal or ordinal) variable to color.



Code
rx <- rnorm(100)
my_colors <- rep(c("color_1", "color_2"), each = 50)
df <- data.frame(rx, my_colors)
ggplot(df) +
  aes(x = rx, fill = my_colors) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30)

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II

title: Work session: Making figures on your own II
text:
Change the axis labels

Using the xlab() and ylab() functions, you can customize the axis labels.
You need to “add” these annotations to your plot using the plus (+) syntax.



Code
rx <- rnorm(100)
my_colors <- rep(c("color_1", "color_2"), each = 50)
df <- data.frame(rx, my_colors)
ggplot(df) +
  aes(x = rx, fill = my_colors) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  xlab("random number") +
  ylab("observed count")

  purrr::quietly()

title: Findings: Data viz outside psych sci
text:
Gathering
Next, we download the data from the Google Sheet where it is collected. Dr. Gilmore has stored his Google account credentials in a special environment file that can be accessed by the R command Sys.getenv("GMAIL_SURVEY").






Tip



It’s vital to be very careful when creating and sharing code like this that involves sensitive information like login credentials.
Gilmore likes to put credentials in an .Renviron file that lives in his home directory. This is a recommended practice. On Mac OS and Linux, that’s ~/.Renviron. You can use the usethis::edit_r_profile() command at the R console (not the Terminal) to open your own .Renviron file. In Gilmore’s case, he has added the following line to that file:
GMAIL_SURVEY="<my-google-account>"
Here, he has substituted his Google account with credentials/access to the required files for <my-google-account>. Then, when the R code below calls Sys.getenv("GMAIL_SURVEY"), the value of those credentials is returned as a text string.
Make sure to close and save the .Renviron file and restart your R session before testing this yourself.




Code
if (!dir.exists('csv')) {
  message("Creating missing `csv/`.")
  dir.create("csv")
}

if (params$update_data) {
  options(gargle_oauth_email = Sys.getenv("GMAIL_SURVEY"))
  googledrive::drive_auth()

  googledrive::drive_download(
    "PSYCH-490.007-Fall-2026-Biz-Govt",
    path = file.path("csv", params$fn),
    type = "csv",
    overwrite = TRUE
  )
  message("Data updated.")
} else {
  message("Using stored data.")
}


The data file has been saved as a comma-separated value (CSV) format data file in a special directory called csv/.






Note



Because these data might contain sensitive or identifiable information, we only keep a local copy and do not share it publicly via GitHub. This is achieved by adding the name of the data directory to a special .gitignore file.

title: Captions and figure numbers
text:
Figure captions
There are several ways to add captions to your Quarto figures depending on how the figures are generated.

R code chunk
If you create a figure using an R code chunk, you can add a caption by using the fig-caption argument in the code chunk options. See Figure 1.



```{r}
#| label: fig-my-plot
#| fig-cap: "This is my plot. I hope that you like it."

x_random <- rnorm(n = 100)
random_df <- data.frame(x = x_random)

random_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Random Data") + 
  theme_minimal()
```


Figure 1: This code shows how to add parameters to an R code chunk. The parameters are preceded by #|. The parameter values are specified as key-value pairs. The key is the label before the colon :, and the value is what follows the colon We need to label figures using #| label: fig-<name>, where the figure name is specified as fig-<name>; here it is my-plot. This makes sure that your Quarto document assigns a unique name to your figure. We also need a #| fig-cap: parameter (cap is short for caption) to add a caption.



The figure rendered by Figure 1 is as follows:


Code
x_random <- rnorm(n = 100)
random_df <- data.frame(x = x_random)

random_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  labs(title = "Histogram of Random Data") + 
  theme_minimal()


`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.








Figure 2: This is my plot. I hope that you like it.











NoteTitles can coexist with captions.



We can make figures with titles using labs(title = "Histogram of Random Data") or the ggtitle() function. The same figure can have a caption added using fig-cap: "This is a caption" in the chunk options.




Images
If you include an image from the internet or a local file, it’s easy to add a caption.
The syntax for adding an image is ![Caption goes  here](url_or_path_to_file_goes_here).
So the following:
![Nittany Lion Shrine from brand.psu.edu.](https://brand.psu.edu/images/backgrounds/warneke-shrine_v1_1.jpg)
yields



Nittany Lion Shrine from brand.psu.edu.








ImportantWhere did the figure number go?



Notice that the above image does not have a figure number, unlike the previous ones. What gives?
The answer is that we need to give the figure its own unique #fig-<name> identifer.


To give an included or embedded image a sequential figure number, we need to add something to the Quarto code that embeds the image. You might have to scroll horizontally to see all of the code.
![Nittany Lion Shrine from brand.psu.edu.](https://brand.psu.edu/images/backgrounds/warneke-shrine_v1_1.jpg){#fig-lion-shrine}
Now that our embedded figure has its own #fig-name, Quarto gives it a sequential figure number. See Figure 3) below.






Figure 3: Nittany Lion Shrine from brand.psu.edu.





Videos, code chunks, etc.
You can turn many bits of Quarto code into figures using a special syntax that wraps the code in pairs of triple colons ::: as shown in Figure 4.



::: {#fig-video}

This is a video from YouTube.
:::

title: ggplot2 tutorial II
text:
Good habits
One of the first things data analysts should do when we get our hands on a new dataset is answer some basic questions about it, specifically the following:

How many cases (data points) are in the dataset?
How many variables?
Which variables are nominal, which are ordinal, and which are continuous?

R makes it easy to answer these questions for us. We use the summary() and dim() (dimension) commands.
Add a section to your Quarto document for summary data about the diamonds dataset. Then, add the following code chunk.



```{r}
summary(diamonds)
```


Figure 3: R code to provide summary information about the diamonds dataset.






```{r}
dim(diamonds)
```


Figure 4: R code to provide summary information about the dimensions of the diamonds dataset.



Save your Quarto document and render it.





     carat               cut        color        clarity          depth

Figure 5: Output from Figure 3 and Figure 4.



Notice that the summary() function does what it says; it provides a statistical summary of the variables in the dataset. For continuous variables, we get the minimum and maximum, the mean and median, and the 1st and 3rd quartile values. For discrete variables (cut, color, and clarity), we get informatoin about the number of cases at each level.
The dim() command tells us that there are 53,940 rows or individual cases and 10 columns or variables. That’s a lot of diamonds!
How do we know whether the discrete variables are ordered?
One way is to use the unique() command. If the dataset has recorded that a variable is ordinal, this command will show us.



```{r}
with(diamonds, unique(cut))

with(diamonds, unique(color))

with(diamonds, unique(clarity))
```


Figure 6: Code to report the number of unique values in a variable and whether they have an intrinsic order.








[1] Ideal     Premium   Good      Very Good Fair     
Levels: Fair < Good < Very Good < Premium < Ideal


[1] E I J H F G D
Levels: D < E < F < G < H < I < J


[1] SI2  SI1  VS1  VS2  VVS2 VVS1 I1   IF  
Levels: I1 < SI2 < SI1 < VS2 < VS1 < VVS2 < VVS1 < IF




Figure 7: Output from Figure 6



You might add this to your document so that you have a reasonably complete summary of the dataset before we visualize it.






WarningConsistency alert



Gilmore usually advocates for a visualize first, analyze later approach to data exploration. But here, we’re generating statistical summaries before we’ve done any visualization. What gives?
Well, Gilmore should probably revise his advice to say summarize before you analyze.

title: ggplot2 tutorial II
text:
Summarizing figures

Continuous data
A best practice is to generate summary figures for all the variables in your dataset. What should the figures summarize, or said in the language of ggplot, what geom_ should we use? Histograms (geom_histogram()), boxplots (geom_boxplot()), and violin (geom_violin()) plots are great for continuous data.
The following code chunk provides these for carat and price.



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = carat) +
  geom_histogram()
  
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = carat, y = "") +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .4) +
  ylab("")
```


Figure 8: Code to generate a histogram and combined boxplot/violin plot of the carat variable.



Create a section of your Quarto document for these figures and make plots for the continuous variables.
Here’s what that should look like:


`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value `binwidth`.








Figure 9: Output from the code in Figure 8.











Figure 10: Output from the code in Figure 8.







Discrete data
But what about nominal (ordered or unordered) data? Will a histogram work here? Let’s try it. Try the code below in your Quarto document.



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = cut) +
  geom_histogram()
```


Figure 11: Code to generate a histogram of the cut variable. Note: This will throw an error.



So, the error message says no, that’s not quite right. But it does give us a hint at what might work. Let’s add stat = "count" to the histogram.



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = cut) +
  geom_histogram(stat = "count")
```


Figure 12: Code to generate a histogram of the cut variable with a changed stat parameter.





Warning in geom_histogram(stat = "count"): Ignoring unknown parameters:
`binwidth` and `bins`








Figure 13: Output from the code in Figure 12.





That looks good.
Let’s do the same thing for color.



```{r}
ggplot(data = diamonds) +
  aes(x = color) +
  geom_histogram(stat = "count")
```


Figure 14: Code to generate a histogram of the color variable with stat = count parameter.





Warning in geom_histogram(stat = "count"): Ignoring unknown parameters:
`binwidth` and `bins`








Figure 15: Output from the code in Figure 14.





That also looks good. Notice that the data are plotted in terms of the order of the color variable, not the category of the variable with the largest number of cases (G). The plot of cut naturally sorted in the same order as the underlying order of cut.
How would we reorder the plot from highest to lowest?
There are several ways to do this. We’re going to use a scheme that will be useful to you in the future.
First, we need to install two new packages. Switch to your R console to do this.



install.packages(c("dplyr", "forcats"))


Figure 16: Code to install the dplyr and forcats packages.



Then, in your Quarto document, add a line to the code chunk in your Setup section so that it looks like the following:



## Setup

Load required packages into the workspace.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)
```


Figure 17: Quarto (and R) code to put at the top of your document so that these libraries are available for later chunks.



With those preliminaries finished, we can now use these libraries to sort the diamonds color data for our summary figure.
Here is the code to add to your Quarto document.



```{r}
diamonds |>
  mutate(color_ct = fct_infreq(color)) |>
                                        
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = color_ct) +
  geom_histogram(stat = "count")

```


Figure 18: Code to render a sorted histogram/barplot of the color variable.



Let’s unpack what’s happening here. First, we give ggplot2 input using a new command, the pipe (|>). Think of the pipe as passing data to the next step. Next, the mutate() function creates a new variable called color_ct, short for color count. The value of color_ct comes from fct_infreq(color), a function in the forcats package. This package has all kinds of useful tools for manipulating factors, both ordered and unordered discrete variable. Learn more about it here. The mutate() command creates a new variable called color_ct using fct_infreq(color) and adds it to the dataset. We then pipe/pass this augmented dataset to ggplot, and the rest should be familiar to you already.

1diamonds |>
2  mutate(color_ct = fct_infreq(color)) |>
  
  ggplot() +
3  aes(x = color_ct) +
  geom_histogram(stat = "count")


1

Pipe/send the diamonds dataset using the pipe |> command.

2

Use mutate() from dplyr and fct_infreq() from forcats to create a new variable called color_ct.

3

Use the new color_ct variable to make the histogram.










Figure 19: Output from the code in Figure 18.











ImportantSorting in a different direction



Read the documentation for the fct_infreq() to see if you can figure out how to print the bars from low to high.
Hint: It involves the use of another forcats function called fct_rev().


If our category labels are more than single letters, it can be easier to rotate the figure. Here’s an easy way to do that.

diamonds |>                               
  mutate(color_ct = fct_infreq(color)) |> 
  
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = color_ct) +                     
  geom_histogram(stat = "count") +
1  coord_flip()


1

“Flip” the coordinates so that the bars are horizontal.










Figure 20: Output from the code in Figure 18.





Let’s put the highest count on top.



```{r}
diamonds |>                               
  mutate(color_ct = fct_rev(fct_infreq(color))) |>
  
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = color_ct) +                     
  geom_histogram(stat = "count") +
  coord_flip()                    
```


Figure 21: Code to flip the coordinates of our histogram.



The following shows what this should look like.

diamonds |>                               
1  mutate(color_ct = fct_rev(fct_infreq(color))) |>
  
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = color_ct) +                     
  geom_histogram(stat = "count") +
  coord_flip()                    


1

Reverse the sort order using fct_rev().










Figure 22: Output from the code in Figure 21.











ImportantWork iteratively



Making figures with code forces us to work one step at a time. That’s a good discipline, but can frustrate people who like to move quickly.
My recommendations are to create the most basic figure for your purpose, then add features (sorting, flipping coordinates, adding color, etc.) one by one. In fact, if you create separate figures for each new addition, then you can always go back to where you started.

title: ggplot2 tutorial II
text:
Putting it all together
You now have enough knowledge to create figures that show the basic distributions of all of the variables in the diamonds dataset.
If you’re feeling ambitious, list other datasets built in to R or one of the packages we’ve used by running data() in the R console.
Pick one, run summary() and dim(), and even try a few simple plots. At this point, I suggest you use the following structure for your code:



```{r}
dataset_name |>
  
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = var_in_dataset) +
  geom_histogram()
```


Figure 23: Gilmore’s recommended template for your plotting code.



This will set you up for success in future data plotting adventures.
Of course, make sure to create a new section in your Quarto document and add some text indicating that you’ve moved to a different dataset. As the saying goes, be kind to your future (forgetful) self. Have fun!






NoteAdding captions



You may notice that your figures do not have captions, but mine do. Adding captions isn’t hard, but I will need to create a separate tutorial for it.
Stay tuned.

title: Making and visualizing data
text:
Nominal data
Let’s focus on nominal or categorical data, specifically the favorite colors of some imaginary set of people.


Code
# Make an array of color names
colors <- c("red", "orange", "yellow", "green", "cyan", "blue", "violet", "white", "black", "gray")


There are n=10 colors in this set.






NoteYour turn



Why are these data nominal or nominally scaled? Or rather, why aren’t they ordinal, interval, or ratio?



Generating
For demonstration purposes, we want to take some number of random samples of these colors. Let’s pick n=200 and sample with replacement (replace=TRUE in the code below), meaning that we could have any number of colors in our sample of 200 imaginary people.


Code
# Use `sample()` to pick a random sample of these *with* replacement so that 
# the numbers/color differ.
our_color_sample <- sample(colors, size=200, replace=TRUE)
our_color_sample
